stem: The Ramsar Convention on Wetlands was adopted in 1971 in the city of Ramsar, which is in:
solution: The Convention on Wetlands was signed in 1971 in Ramsar, Iran. It is the oldest of the modern global intergovernmental environmental agreements and provides the framework for conservation and wise use of wetlands.

stem: Under the Ramsar Convention, the criterion for selecting a wetland of international importance based on waterbirds is that it regularly supports at least:
solution: A wetland qualifies if it regularly supports 20,000 or more waterbirds, or 1% of the individuals in a population of one species/subspecies of waterbird, among the nine Ramsar criteria.

stem: The list of Ramsar sites in danger of losing their ecological character due to human interference is called the:
solution: The Montreux Record lists Ramsar sites where changes in ecological character have occurred or are likely due to technological development, pollution or human interference. Keoladeo and Loktak (India) have featured on it.

stem: 'Wise use' — the central concept of the Ramsar Convention — essentially means:
options: Total prohibition of all human use
Maintenance of a wetland's ecological character through sustainable use
solution: 'Wise use' is defined as maintaining the ecological character of wetlands through ecosystem approaches within the context of sustainable development — balancing conservation with human use.

stem: Which of the following is NOT considered a wetland under the broad Ramsar definition?
solution: Ramsar defines wetlands broadly to include marshes, peatlands, mangroves, coral reefs, rivers, lakes, and even shallow marine areas up to 6 m depth at low tide. A tilled dryland farm is not a wetland.

stem: India's first two Ramsar sites, designated in 1981, were Chilika Lake (Odisha) and:
solution: Chilika Lake and Keoladeo National Park (Bharatpur) were India's first Ramsar sites, both designated in 1981.

stem: Chilika Lake, India's largest coastal (brackish-water) lagoon and a Ramsar site, is located in:
solution: Chilika in Odisha is Asia's largest brackish-water lagoon, wintering ground for migratory birds and home to the endangered Irrawaddy dolphin.

stem: The Irrawaddy dolphin in India is chiefly associated with which Ramsar lagoon?
solution: Chilika Lake harbours one of the few populations of the vulnerable Irrawaddy dolphin, a key conservation attraction of the lagoon.

stem: Wular Lake, one of Asia's largest freshwater lakes and a Ramsar site, lies in:
solution: Wular Lake in Jammu & Kashmir is one of the largest freshwater lakes in Asia, fed by the Jhelum; it plays a flood-absorption role and is a Ramsar site.

stem: Loktak Lake, famous for its floating 'phumdis' and Keibul Lamjao National Park, is a Ramsar site in:
solution: Loktak in Manipur is the largest freshwater lake in Northeast India, noted for floating phumdis (mats of vegetation) and the sangai's habitat at Keibul Lamjao. It was placed on the Montreux Record.

stem: Keoladeo National Park (Bharatpur), a Ramsar site and UNESCO World Heritage Site, is historically famous as a wintering ground for the (now rarely seen) migratory:
solution: Keoladeo was a celebrated wintering site for the critically endangered Siberian crane and hosts thousands of migratory waterbirds. It is a man-made/managed wetland.

stem: Sambhar Lake, India's largest inland saline (salt) lake and a Ramsar site, is in:
solution: Sambhar Lake near Jaipur, Rajasthan, is India's largest inland salt lake, a major salt-production site and a Ramsar wetland attracting flamingos.

stem: As of the mid-2020s, India has the largest network of Ramsar sites in Asia, numbering (approximately):
solution: India crossed 80 Ramsar sites by 2024, the highest in Asia and among the highest in the world, reflecting rapid recent designations (Tamil Nadu and UP lead in numbers).

stem: The primary body providing scientific and technical advice to the Ramsar Convention is the:
solution: The Scientific and Technical Review Panel (STRP) advises the Ramsar Convention on scientific and technical matters. The Convention is administered from Gland, Switzerland.

stem: The key ecological services of wetlands include all EXCEPT:
solution: Wetlands recharge aquifers, buffer floods, filter pollutants, sequester carbon (especially peatlands), and support biodiversity — they are called 'kidneys of the landscape'. They mitigate, not accelerate, desertification.

stem: Wetlands in India are legally protected under which set of rules?
solution: The Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 (under the Environment Protection Act, 1986) regulate activities in notified wetlands and empower State Wetland Authorities.

stem: Eutrophication, a major threat to wetlands and lakes, is caused primarily by:
options: Nutrient enrichment (nitrogen and phosphorus) leading to algal blooms
solution: Nutrient over-enrichment (mainly N and P from fertilisers/sewage) triggers algal blooms; their decay depletes oxygen, killing aquatic life. This is eutrophication, a leading cause of wetland degradation.

stem: Mangroves are salt-tolerant plants of the intertidal zone. Their specialised aerial roots that emerge for gas exchange are called:
solution: Mangroves develop pneumatophores (breathing roots) that project above waterlogged, oxygen-poor mud to obtain oxygen. Many are also viviparous (seeds germinate on the parent plant).

stem: The largest mangrove forest in India (and the world) is the:
solution: The Sundarbans (West Bengal, shared with Bangladesh) is the world's largest single block of mangrove, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and Ramsar wetland, home to the Royal Bengal tiger.

stem: Coral reefs are built by colonies of tiny animals called polyps that live in symbiosis with photosynthetic algae known as:
solution: Reef-building coral polyps host symbiotic zooxanthellae (dinoflagellate algae) that supply food via photosynthesis and give corals their colour. Loss of zooxanthellae causes coral bleaching.

stem: Coral bleaching occurs when:
options: Stressed corals expel their symbiotic zooxanthellae, turning white
solution: Under stress (chiefly warming seas), corals expel their zooxanthellae, losing colour and their main food source; prolonged bleaching leads to coral death. Rising sea temperature from climate change is the primary driver.

stem: Corals thrive best under which set of conditions?
options: Warm, shallow, clear, well-lit tropical marine water of normal salinity
solution: Reef-building corals need warm (23–29°C), shallow, clear, sunlit, oxygen-rich saline tropical/subtropical waters so their zooxanthellae can photosynthesise; sediment and freshwater harm them.

stem: India's major coral reef areas include the Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, Lakshadweep and:
solution: India's four major reef regions are the Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, Lakshadweep (atolls) and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands (fringing reefs).

stem: The three main types of coral reefs are fringing reefs, barrier reefs and:
solution: Coral reefs are classified as fringing reefs (attached to shore), barrier reefs (separated from shore by a lagoon) and atolls (ring-shaped reefs enclosing a lagoon, e.g. Lakshadweep).

stem: Estuaries — where rivers meet the sea — are highly productive because they:
options: Trap nutrients and support high biological productivity as nurseries
solution: Estuaries mix fresh and salt water, trapping nutrients and sediment; they act as nurseries for many fish and shellfish, ranking among the most productive ecosystems on Earth.

stem: The open ocean zone of sunlit surface water where photosynthesis occurs is the:
solution: The photic (euphotic) zone is the sunlit upper layer where phytoplankton photosynthesise, driving marine food webs; below it lies the aphotic (dark) zone.

stem: Phytoplankton are ecologically vital because they:
options: Form the base of most marine food chains and produce much of Earth's oxygen
solution: Phytoplankton (microscopic algae) are the primary producers of the ocean, base of marine food webs and responsible for roughly half of global photosynthetic oxygen production.

stem: Upwelling zones in the ocean are highly productive fisheries because:
options: Nutrient-rich deep water rises to the sunlit surface
solution: Upwelling brings cold, nutrient-rich deep water to the surface, fuelling phytoplankton blooms and rich fisheries (e.g. off Peru). It is a key link between ocean circulation and productivity.

stem: A 'harmful algal bloom' producing toxins that discolour water is popularly called a:
solution: Red tides are harmful algal blooms (often dinoflagellates) that discolour coastal water and release toxins, killing fish and contaminating shellfish. They are worsened by nutrient pollution.

stem: Ocean acidification, a threat to corals and shellfish, is caused by the ocean absorbing excess:
solution: The ocean absorbs about a quarter of anthropogenic CO2; it reacts with seawater to form carbonic acid, lowering pH and reducing carbonate ions needed by corals, molluscs and plankton to build shells/skeletons.

stem: Seagrass meadows and mangroves are important 'blue carbon' ecosystems because they:
options: Sequester and store large amounts of carbon in coastal sediments
Only store carbon in the air
solution: 'Blue carbon' refers to carbon captured by coastal/marine ecosystems — mangroves, seagrasses and salt marshes — which store carbon in biomass and waterlogged sediments far longer than many terrestrial forests.

stem: The Montreal-style 'dead zones' in oceans (e.g. off the coasts) are areas of:
options: Hypoxia (very low oxygen) caused by eutrophication
solution: Dead zones are hypoxic (oxygen-depleted) areas, typically caused by nutrient runoff triggering algal blooms whose decomposition consumes oxygen, making waters uninhabitable for most marine life.

stem: The Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve is notable for protecting which trio of coastal ecosystems?
options: Coral reefs, seagrass beds and mangroves
solution: The Gulf of Mannar (Tamil Nadu), India's first marine biosphere reserve, protects coral reefs, seagrass meadows, mangroves, dugongs and diverse marine fauna.

stem: The dugong (sea cow), India's only herbivorous marine mammal, depends primarily on:
solution: The vulnerable dugong grazes on seagrass; its Indian strongholds are the Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch and Andaman & Nicobar. A dedicated dugong conservation reserve has been notified in the Palk Bay.

stem: Which of the following statements about mangroves is correct? (i) They stabilise coastlines and reduce erosion (ii) They act as a buffer against storm surges and tsunamis (iii) They are nurseries for fish
solution: Mangroves provide all three services — trapping sediment and stabilising coasts, absorbing wave/storm and tsunami energy, and serving as nurseries for fish and crustaceans — besides sequestering blue carbon.

stem: 'MISHTI' (2023) is a Government of India scheme for the conservation of:
options: Mangroves along the coastline and on salt-pan lands
solution: MISHTI (Mangrove Initiative for Shoreline Habitats & Tangible Incomes), launched in 2023, promotes mangrove plantation and restoration along India's coastline and salt-pan lands.

stem: The 'Amrit Dharohar' initiative (2023) focuses on the conservation and 'wise use' of:
solution: Amrit Dharohar (2023) promotes the optimal use and conservation of Ramsar wetlands, enhancing biodiversity, eco-tourism and local livelihoods.

stem: Peatlands are important because, despite covering only ~3% of land, they store:
options: More carbon than all the world's forests combined (roughly twice the forest carbon)
solution: Peatlands (a type of wetland with accumulated partially decayed organic matter) store enormous quantities of carbon — about twice that stored in all forests — making their drainage a major source of CO2 emissions.

stem: Pulicat Lake, India's second-largest brackish-water lagoon and a flamingo haven, straddles the borders of:
solution: Pulicat Lake lies across Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu; it is India's second-largest brackish lagoon after Chilika and hosts flamingos and the Nelapattu bird sanctuary nearby.

stem: The National Plan for Conservation of Aquatic Ecosystems (NPCA) merges two earlier schemes covering:
solution: The NPCA integrates the erstwhile National Wetland Conservation Programme and National Lake Conservation Plan to holistically conserve wetlands and lakes across India.

stem: Which of the following best explains why wetlands are called 'kidneys of the landscape'?
options: They filter and purify water by trapping sediments and breaking down pollutants
solution: Like kidneys, wetlands cleanse water — trapping sediments, absorbing nutrients and breaking down or immobilising pollutants — improving downstream water quality.

stem: The 'World Wetlands Day' is observed annually on:
solution: World Wetlands Day is marked on 2 February, the anniversary of the signing of the Ramsar Convention in 1971.

stem: Mangrove destruction increases coastal vulnerability chiefly by removing a natural barrier against:
solution: Mangroves dissipate wave energy; their loss exposes coasts to greater damage from cyclones, storm surges and tsunamis — evident in the differential 2004 tsunami impact where mangroves survived.

stem: Which Indian state has the largest number of Ramsar sites (as of the mid-2020s)?
solution: Tamil Nadu, following a rapid spate of designations, holds the highest number of Ramsar sites among Indian states, followed by Uttar Pradesh.

stem: Salt marshes, mudflats and mangroves are all examples of:
solution: Salt marshes, tidal mudflats, mangroves, coral reefs, estuaries and lagoons are coastal and marine wetlands, distinct from inland (rivers, lakes, marshes, peatlands) and human-made (reservoirs, tanks) wetlands.

stem: Ecologically, coral reefs are often called 'rainforests of the sea' because they:
options: Harbour extraordinarily high marine biodiversity despite covering under 1% of the ocean floor
solution: Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor yet support about a quarter of all marine species, giving them biodiversity comparable to tropical rainforests.

stem: The Deepor Beel Ramsar site, an important freshwater lake and bird habitat, is located near which city?
solution: Deepor Beel, a permanent freshwater lake southwest of Guwahati, Assam, is a Ramsar site and important bird area, though threatened by encroachment and pollution.

stem: Which factor is the single greatest driver of coral bleaching events worldwide?
options: Rising sea surface temperature due to global warming
solution: Marine heatwaves from global warming are the dominant cause of mass coral bleaching; even a 1–2°C rise above summer maxima for a few weeks can trigger widespread bleaching.

stem: Constructed/man-made wetlands are increasingly used for:
solution: Constructed wetlands use plants, soil and microbes to treat sewage and wastewater cheaply and naturally — e.g. the East Kolkata Wetlands (a Ramsar site) treat the city's sewage and support fisheries.

stem: The East Kolkata Wetlands, a Ramsar site, are globally recognised as a model of:
options: Resource-recovery: using city sewage for fisheries and agriculture
solution: The East Kolkata Wetlands naturally treat Kolkata's sewage and reuse the nutrient-rich water for fish farming and vegetable cultivation — a celebrated example of a working, productive wetland ('wise use').

stem: Wetlands are broadly defined as areas where water covers the soil or is present at or near the surface for at least part of the year, making the soil:
solution: Wetlands feature water-saturated (hydric) soils and water-adapted (hydrophytic) vegetation, sitting at the interface of terrestrial and aquatic systems.

stem: The Ramsar Convention's official name is the Convention on Wetlands of International Importance especially as:
solution: Its full title is the Convention on Wetlands of International Importance especially as Waterfowl Habitat, reflecting its origin in concern for migratory waterbird conservation.

stem: The theme day and framework of the Ramsar Convention emphasise which core idea?
solution: 'Wise use' — maintaining wetlands' ecological character through sustainable, ecosystem-based approaches — is the guiding principle of the Ramsar Convention.

stem: Which Indian wetland is a Ramsar site AND famous for the largest congregation of migratory birds in an urban lake near Bhopal?
solution: The Bhoj Wetland (Upper and Lower Lakes) in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh, is a Ramsar site and important urban wetland supporting rich birdlife.

stem: The Sundarbans wetland (a Ramsar site) is critically important as a:
options: Mangrove ecosystem and tiger habitat buffering cyclones
solution: The Sundarbans Ramsar site protects the world's largest mangrove forest, home to the Royal Bengal tiger, and buffers the coast against cyclones and storm surges.

stem: 'Point Calimere' Wildlife and Bird Sanctuary, a Ramsar site with flamingos and mudflats, is in:
solution: Point Calimere (Kodiakkarai) in Tamil Nadu is a Ramsar site with coastal wetlands, mudflats and salt swamps attracting flamingos and other migratory birds.

stem: Which of the following ecosystem services do wetlands NOT typically provide?
solution: Wetlands buffer floods, recharge groundwater, purify water, store carbon and support biodiversity; they have no role in producing atmospheric ozone.

stem: 'Anthropogenic' threats to wetlands in India include all EXCEPT:
solution: Wetlands are threatened by encroachment, drainage, pollution, siltation, invasive species and over-extraction. Natural rainfall sustains, not threatens, them.

stem: Loktak Lake's floating 'phumdis' are:
options: Heterogeneous masses of vegetation, soil and organic matter in various stages of decomposition floating on the water
solution: Phumdis are floating mats of vegetation and organic matter on Loktak Lake; the largest phumdi forms Keibul Lamjao National Park, the sangai's habitat.

stem: Chilika Lake was placed on and later removed from the Montreux Record after successful:
options: Restoration (opening a new sea mouth to restore salinity and ecology)
solution: Chilika was on the Montreux Record due to siltation and shrinking; opening a new sea mouth restored its salinity, fisheries and birdlife, and it was removed from the Record — a global restoration success.

stem: 'Renuka Lake', India's Ramsar wetland shaped like a reclining woman, is in:
solution: Renuka Lake in Himachal Pradesh is a Ramsar site and the largest natural lake in the state, of cultural and ecological importance.

stem: Coral polyps belong to which animal phylum?
solution: Corals are cnidarians (like jellyfish and sea anemones), building calcium carbonate skeletons that accumulate into reefs over time.

stem: Coral reefs form best in waters that are:
options: Warm, shallow, clear and of normal marine salinity
solution: Reef corals need warm (23–29°C), shallow, clear, sunlit and normal-salinity seawater so their symbiotic zooxanthellae can photosynthesise.

stem: An 'atoll' is a coral reef that is:
options: Ring-shaped, enclosing a central lagoon (often around a sunken island)
solution: An atoll is a ring-shaped coral reef enclosing a lagoon, typically formed around a subsiding volcanic island — Lakshadweep's coral islands are atolls.

stem: Lakshadweep islands are made up of which reef type?
solution: The Lakshadweep islands are coral atolls in the Arabian Sea — the only coral atolls in India — highly vulnerable to sea-level rise and bleaching.

stem: Ocean acidification harms coral reefs because it:
options: Reduces the availability of carbonate ions needed to build calcium carbonate skeletons
solution: Dissolved CO2 lowers seawater pH and carbonate ion concentration, making it harder for corals (and shellfish) to build and maintain their calcium carbonate structures.

stem: 'Blue carbon' ecosystems include mangroves, seagrasses and:
solution: Blue carbon ecosystems — mangroves, seagrass meadows and tidal salt marshes — sequester and store large amounts of carbon in their biomass and waterlogged sediments.

stem: Seagrasses differ from seaweeds (algae) in that seagrasses are:
options: True flowering plants with roots, stems and flowers
solution: Seagrasses are true flowering (marine) plants with roots, stems, leaves and flowers, unlike seaweeds which are algae. Seagrass meadows are vital blue-carbon and dugong habitats.

stem: The 'Gulf of Mannar' between India and Sri Lanka is India's first:
solution: The Gulf of Mannar Marine Biosphere Reserve (Tamil Nadu), established in 1989, was India's first marine biosphere reserve, protecting coral reefs, seagrass, mangroves and dugongs.

stem: Mangroves reproduce by 'vivipary', which means the:
options: Seeds germinate while still attached to the parent plant
solution: Many mangroves are viviparous — their seeds germinate on the parent tree, forming propagules that drop and root quickly in soft mud, an adaptation to the unstable intertidal zone.

stem: Bhitarkanika, an important mangrove and Ramsar site, hosts the largest Indian population of:
solution: Bhitarkanika in Odisha shelters India's largest population of the saltwater crocodile, along with rich mangroves and Olive Ridley turtle nesting at nearby Gahirmatha.

stem: The 'kidneys of the landscape' metaphor for wetlands refers to their ability to:
options: Filter and purify water, trapping sediments and pollutants
solution: Like kidneys, wetlands cleanse water by trapping sediments, absorbing nutrients and breaking down or immobilising pollutants, improving downstream water quality.

stem: The productivity of estuaries is high because they:
options: Receive nutrients from rivers and tides, acting as nurseries for many marine species
solution: Estuaries mix nutrient-rich river water with the sea, trapping nutrients and providing sheltered nurseries for fish and shellfish — among the most productive ecosystems.

stem: 'Mangrove for the Future' and MISHTI are initiatives that reflect growing recognition of mangroves' role in:
options: Coastal protection, blue carbon and livelihoods
solution: Such initiatives promote mangrove conservation and restoration for their coastal-protection, carbon-storage, fisheries and livelihood benefits, e.g. India's MISHTI scheme (2023).

stem: India's Ramsar site count crossing 80 makes it hold the largest network of Ramsar sites in:
solution: With over 80 Ramsar sites, India has the largest network in Asia and one of the largest globally, following rapid designations especially in Tamil Nadu and Uttar Pradesh.

stem: The Harike Wetland, a Ramsar site at the confluence of the Beas and Sutlej rivers, lies in:
solution: Harike Wetland in Punjab, formed at the Beas–Sutlej confluence, is a major Ramsar site and refuge for migratory birds and the Indus river dolphin.

stem: The Indus river dolphin, a rare freshwater dolphin, is found in India chiefly in the:
solution: A small population of the endangered Indus river dolphin survives in the Beas river in Punjab, making the Harike–Beas stretch critical for its conservation.

stem: Corals are called 'ecosystem engineers' because they:
options: Build the physical reef structure that provides habitat for countless marine species
solution: By secreting calcium carbonate, corals construct the three-dimensional reef framework that shelters a quarter of all marine species — engineering the habitat that supports reef ecosystems.

stem: A major threat to seagrass meadows and coral reefs from land is:
options: Sedimentation and nutrient runoff from coastal development and agriculture
solution: Sediment and nutrient runoff from land smothers corals, blocks light needed by seagrasses and zooxanthellae, and promotes algal overgrowth — degrading these coastal ecosystems.

stem: 'Salt marshes' are coastal wetlands dominated by:
options: Salt-tolerant grasses and herbaceous plants in the intertidal zone
solution: Salt marshes are intertidal wetlands dominated by salt-tolerant grasses and herbs; they protect coasts, filter water and store blue carbon, common in temperate estuaries and parts of Gujarat.

stem: The Chilika lagoon supports which internationally significant winter migratory phenomenon?
options: Congregation of lakhs of migratory waterbirds from as far as Siberia
solution: Chilika hosts one of the largest congregations of migratory birds on the subcontinent in winter, drawing waterfowl from Siberia, the Caspian and Central Asia, besides its Irrawaddy dolphins.

stem: 'Nalsarovar', a Ramsar bird sanctuary and wetland, is located in:
solution: Nalsarovar in Gujarat is a Ramsar site and large freshwater/brackish wetland famed for migratory birds including flamingos, pelicans and cranes.

stem: Which of the following correctly matches a Ramsar site with its state? (i) Loktak – Manipur (ii) Wular – J&K (iii) Chilika – Odisha
solution: All three are correct: Loktak (Manipur), Wular (Jammu & Kashmir) and Chilika (Odisha) are all designated Ramsar sites.

stem: 'Zooxanthellae' provide corals with:
options: Food (via photosynthesis) and colour, in a mutualistic relationship
solution: Zooxanthellae (symbiotic algae) photosynthesise inside coral tissues, supplying most of the coral's food and giving it colour; their loss under stress causes bleaching.

stem: The 'East Kolkata Wetlands' are globally cited as a model of:
options: Natural sewage treatment and resource recovery (fisheries + agriculture)
solution: The East Kolkata Wetlands (a Ramsar site) naturally treat the city's sewage and reuse the nutrient-rich water for fish farming and vegetable cultivation — a celebrated 'wise use' model.

stem: Mangroves are highly productive and support fisheries because they:
options: Serve as breeding and nursery grounds for fish, prawns and crabs
solution: Mangrove root systems provide sheltered, nutrient-rich nurseries for juvenile fish, prawns and crabs, sustaining coastal fisheries and livelihoods.

stem: The single greatest global threat to coral reefs is:
options: Climate-change-driven ocean warming causing mass bleaching (with acidification)
solution: Rising sea temperatures from global warming trigger mass coral bleaching, while ocean acidification impairs skeleton-building — together the foremost threats to reefs worldwide.

stem: 'Deepor Beel' near Guwahati is significant as a:
options: Freshwater Ramsar wetland and important bird area
solution: Deepor Beel in Assam is a permanent freshwater lake, Ramsar site and important bird area, though threatened by encroachment, waste dumping and a nearby railway.

stem: 'Mangroves' can survive in saline water partly because they:
options: Excrete or exclude excess salt (e.g. through salt glands) and have specialised roots
solution: Mangroves cope with salinity via salt-excreting glands, salt exclusion at the roots, and pneumatophores for oxygen in waterlogged mud — remarkable adaptations to the intertidal zone.

stem: The 'Vembanad-Kol' wetland, India's longest lake and a Ramsar site, is in:
solution: The Vembanad-Kol wetland in Kerala, the state's largest lake and part of the backwaters, is a Ramsar site supporting fisheries, agriculture and rich birdlife.

stem: Which statement about wetlands and climate is correct?
options: Wetlands (especially peatlands and mangroves) store large amounts of carbon, but drained wetlands emit it
solution: Intact wetlands are significant carbon sinks (peatlands and mangroves store vast carbon), but when drained or degraded they release stored carbon as greenhouse gases.

stem: 'Sasthamkotta Lake', a Ramsar site and Kerala's largest freshwater lake, is important for:
options: Drinking water supply and unique biodiversity
solution: Sasthamkotta Lake in Kerala is a Ramsar site providing drinking water to the region and hosting unique fauna, including a larva (Cavaborus) that keeps the water free of bacteria.

stem: 'Keshopur-Miani', 'Nangal' and 'Ropar' are Ramsar wetlands located in:
solution: Keshopur-Miani, Nangal and Ropar (along with Harike) are Ramsar sites in Punjab, reflecting the state's rich network of riverine and man-made wetlands.

stem: The overall function of a lagoon like Chilika or Pulicat is that it is a:
options: Shallow brackish-water body separated from the sea by a sandbar/spit
solution: A coastal lagoon is a shallow brackish-water body partly separated from the sea by a barrier (sandbar/spit), mixing fresh and marine water and supporting rich biodiversity and fisheries.

stem: Which of the following is a primary reason coral reefs are ecologically and economically valuable? (i) Fisheries (ii) Coastal protection (iii) Tourism
solution: Reefs support fisheries, protect coastlines by dissipating wave energy, and draw tourism — besides their immense biodiversity — making them highly valuable ecologically and economically.

stem: The main reason mangroves reduced tsunami/cyclone damage in some coastal areas is that they:
options: Physically dissipate wave and surge energy, acting as a natural barrier
solution: Dense mangrove belts absorb and dissipate the energy of waves, storm surges and tsunamis, reducing their inland impact — a natural coastal defence highlighted after the 2004 tsunami.

stem: Wetlands support 'denitrification', which benefits water quality by:
options: Removing excess nitrogen (converting nitrates to nitrogen gas), reducing eutrophication downstream
solution: Wetland microbes carry out denitrification, converting nitrate pollution into harmless nitrogen gas, thereby cleansing water and reducing downstream eutrophication.

stem: The ecological character of a Ramsar site refers to its:
options: Combination of ecosystem components, processes and services that define the wetland
solution: 'Ecological character' is the sum of the wetland's biological, physical and chemical components and the ecosystem services they provide; maintaining it is the essence of 'wise use'.

stem: Which factor makes India's high-altitude wetlands (e.g. Tso Kar, Tsomoriri in Ladakh) special?
options: They are cold-desert wetlands important for rare birds like the black-necked crane
solution: Ladakh's high-altitude Ramsar wetlands (Tsomoriri, Tso Kar) are cold-desert lakes and vital breeding grounds for the black-necked crane and bar-headed goose.
